+# Spawning Codex CLI inside a Claude cloud session
+Measured on `@openai/codex` 0.153.4 in the Claude Code Remote container,
+2026-09-09, while building the in-session plan reviewer
+(`core/scripts/plan-review.mjs`, workstream #66). Each of these was found by
+hitting it, and each one's symptom points somewhere other than its cause.
+## 1. `codex exec` waits forever on an open stdin
+The Bash tool leaves stdin open. `codex exec` with no prompt argument reads
+instructions from stdin, and an open-but-silent stdin is not EOF — so it waits,
+producing no output, until the tool times out.
+**The symptom is "the model is being slow."** It is not; nothing has been sent.
+Two working shapes:
+```bash
+codex exec "the prompt" </dev/null      # prompt as an argument, stdin closed
+printf '%s' "$prompt" | codex exec -    # `-` reads the prompt from stdin
+From Node, `spawnSync(..., { input: prompt, stdio: ["pipe", ...] })` writes the
+stream and closes it, which is the same thing done properly. `plan-review.mjs`
+uses that shape and passes `-` last for the same reason.
+## 2. `--sandbox read-only` blocks `/tmp`, not just the repo
+The read-only sandbox is not "read the repo, write nowhere else" — it denies
+writes **everywhere**, `/tmp` included. So an agent told to run the project's
+test suite gets `EROFS` from the test runner's own scratch files, which reads
+like a broken checkout rather than a sandbox policy.
+The pilot hit exactly this: the reviewer tried the suite, failed on `/tmp`, and
+honestly recorded it under `unable_to_verify` instead of guessing — which is the
+behaviour you want, but it costs a section of the review.
+If the spawned agent genuinely must run a suite: `--sandbox workspace-write` on
+a **scratch checkout** (a `git worktree`, never the live tree), or set `TMPDIR`
+to a writable directory inside the workspace. If it only needs to read and
+grep — which is what plan review needs — leave it `read-only`.
+## 3. A long run needs `setsid nohup` and an exit file, not a foreground wait
+One `xhigh` review round measured **522 seconds**. That is longer than a
+comfortable Bash tool call, and a foreground run that gets cut off leaves no
+result at all.
+```bash
+setsid nohup bash -c "cd $DIR && codex exec … >$DIR/run.log 2>&1; echo \$? >$DIR/run.exit" \
+  >/dev/null 2>&1 &
+Then poll for `run.exit` — its existence is the completion signal and its
+contents are the status. Two details that cost time here:
+- **Use absolute paths inside the `bash -c`.** The Bash tool resets the working
+  directory between calls, and a `cd` in the launching command does not survive
+  into the detached child the way you expect. The first attempt wrote its log
+  to a directory that no longer applied and looked like a process that never
+  started.
+- **Read the answer from a file, never from the transcript.** `codex exec`
+  prints every tool call it makes (45 of them in the pilot). Use
+  `--output-last-message <file>` and read that; scraping stdout for JSON is a
+  parser you will have to maintain against a transcript format you do not own.
+## 4. `pkill -f 'codex exec'` kills the shell that runs it
+`-f` matches against the full command line, and the shell running
+`pkill -f 'codex exec'` has `codex exec` in **its own** command line. It matches
+itself and dies. The session's Bash tool call ends with no output and no
+explanation.
+Match the binary path instead (`pkill -f '/node_modules/.bin/codex'`), or record
+the PID when you launch it and kill that.
+## 5. Two flags that are not tidiness
+- **`--ignore-user-config`.** `--output-schema` is **ignored when MCP tools are
+  active**, and a user `config.toml` is how MCP tools get turned on. So a schema
+  that silently stops constraining the output is one stray config file away.
+  Auth still reads from `CODEX_HOME`, so this does not disturb the sign-in.
+- **`--ephemeral`.** No session file on disk, which makes "fresh context every
+  round" structural rather than a convention someone remembers.
+## 6. `codex login status` exits 1 and says "Not logged in"
+Both signals are available and both are worth reading — an exit code is a thin
+thing to hang a refusal on. Sign-in in a cloud session is **per session, by
+device code, and never stored**; see
+[`web-research.md`](../../docs/ai-context/web-research.md). The device code
+expires in about 15 minutes, so issue it and ask for approval in the same turn
+rather than preparing work first.

-and the "plan approval is explicit only" rule stay resident in `CLAUDE.md`.
-## The plan-review PR is the plan's delivery surface
-The loop commits the plan to `docs/plans/PLAN_<SLUG>.md` on the
-`plan-review/<slug>` branch, so GitHub renders it as formatted markdown at a
-stable, forwardable URL — that PR page is what David reads, links to, and
-forwards (he works from the iPad web UI, where the plan/chat panel is awkward
-to capture or share). The two older delivery rituals — a markdown hand-off via
-`SendUserFile` (once a hard precondition on `ExitPlanMode`) and a private
-Artifact page — are **retired (David, 2026-07-28)**: he only ever needed the
-markdown for sharing, and the PR page covers both needs. So for a plan going

-revision.
-**The one case that still needs a hand-off:** a plan that never enters the public
-PR channel — the security/confidentiality carve-out, or a genuinely broken loop

-David to read, so **there** I write the markdown out and deliver it via
-`SendUserFile`. That is the exception, not the default; I say plainly that I'm on
-the fallback path when I use it.

-      reviewed at round 4 is reviewed material by round 5, exactly like
-      anything else.
-    - **Unreviewed scope** — added since the *most recent* round, so no round
-      has attacked it yet. Forking it costs **nothing**, because there is no

-    because it is a size judgment, not a review-completeness one.** If

text: name: The machinery's threat model is my own mistakes, not an adversary — a local script is not a security boundary

description: Ten review rounds on AI-Handbook PR #7 hardened repository identity against an attacker who can edit the working tree, commit to the branch, or substitute another repository's receipts. That attacker is me. The controls against deliberate action are David's merge and GitHub's server-side ruleset; the scripts exist to catch mistakes, and designing them to resist their own operator produced three trust anchors, eleven findings, and no additional safety.
<!-- SYNCED FROM AI-Handbook — do not edit in a consumer repo. Local edits are overwritten by the next sync and their reasoning is lost; change the handbook instead. -->
# The machinery's threat model is my own mistakes, not an adversary — a local script is not a security boundary
## What happened
Making the review-budget guard and the readiness gate portable meant
replacing two hardcoded literals — the repository's `owner/name` and the
list of required CI jobs — with configuration. That is a configuration
problem. It was treated as a security problem, and it grew into one.
Each round of review asked "what if the working tree is edited before this
read?", "what if a same-numbered PR from another repository supplies its
snapshot?", "what if the branch commits a weaker policy than `main`?" — and
each answer moved the read somewhere harder to reach: from the working tree
to the durable ref, from the durable ref to the base commit, from a config
value to the budget receipt beside it. By round ten there were three
different trust anchors for one identity, a classification file ranking
their trustworthiness, and Codex was correctly finding the gaps *between*
the anchors, which is a combinatorial space. Every finding was real under
its own premise. The premise was wrong.
The premise was that the scripts must resist the person running them. In
this environment there is exactly one actor: the agent that edits the
working tree, commits to the branch, captures the snapshot, runs the gate
and posts the review request. Whatever it can "attack" it can also simply
not run. The controls that exist against deliberate action are outside the
scripts entirely — a human's merge click, and the server-side ruleset on
`main` — and no local hook can add to them, because the hook's operator is
the party being controlled.
## What worked instead
State the job plainly and design for it: **the identity checks catch
mistakes.** Declaring a budget in the wrong checkout. Capturing the wrong
PR's snapshot because every repository has a #7. Running a gate in a
consumer that still carries the seed placeholder. Those are the failures
that actually happen, and every one is caught by the same simple shape:
1. **One reader.** `.agents/machinery.json` is read from the working tree,
because it is configuration and that is where configuration lives. One
function reads it; it fails closed on absent, malformed, or placeholder.
2. **Stamp on mint, compare on consume.** Every artifact the machinery
writes carries `repo` from that config. Every artifact it reads is
compared to it. A mismatch refuses with "minted for X, you are in Y."
3. **GitHub's word is compared to config too.** A snapshot naming another
repository is refused: you captured the wrong PR.
4. **No trust hierarchy.** Not "base commit beats durable ref beats working
tree." One source, compared everywhere. (Receipts are still read from
the durable ref — for *durability*, so a decision survives the container,
which is a different concern that predates this one.)
5. **The guard path reads no config**, for an operational reason, not a
trust one: an exception escaping the hook exits 1 and the tool call
proceeds. There, the budget receipt is the anchor.
A finding of the shape "an edit to the working tree could…" is declined by
pointing here. It is not a defect in a mistake-catcher that its operator can
disable it.
## Takeaway
Before hardening a check, name the actor it is hardening against. If the
answer is "the person who runs it," stop: you are designing a lock whose key
is on the same ring, and every layer you add is a place for two copies of
the same value to disagree. Ask instead what mistake the check catches, make
it catch that mistake in one obvious way, and put the real control — a
human's approval, a server-side rule — where a local script cannot reach it.

body: **<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Add a budget mechanism for PR-less plan loops**

The new workflow removes the plan-review PR but says its budget and David gate remain unchanged. The only documented/enforced budget machinery is PR-keyed: `review-budget.mjs` requires `--pr`, reads receipts from a remote-tracking branch, and `review-loop-record.mjs` also needs a PR snapshot; `plan-review.mjs` performs no budget check itself. Consequently a local plan loop has no way to declare or enforce its cap, dispatch the cap adjudication, or write the promised `loop-extension-<pr>-<n>.json`, so this safety gate is either unusable or silently manual in every consumer.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate reconciliation IDs before accepting a round**

When `--prior` supplies findings, schema validation accepts any `previous_findings` array without comparing its IDs to the supplied priors; for example, a response with `previous_findings: []` or duplicate/unrelated IDs passes here. Because convergence depends on every prior being returned as `Resolved` or `Superseded`, a model omission can yield an accepted assessment that appears clean without reconciling the open issue. Cross-check the returned IDs one-for-one against `priors` before writing the round JSON.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Require round-zero concerns on round one**

The skill says round-zero `scope_concerns` carry into round 1, but this condition permits round 1 with neither `--prior` nor `--no-prior`, and the documented round-1 command does exactly that. Whenever the scope reviewer returns a concern, the first plan review therefore receives an empty prior list and cannot reconcile whether the plan addressed it. Require an explicit prior/no-prior choice starting at round 1 and show `--prior` in the round-1 invocation.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Remove stale output before a forced rerun**

With `--force`, an existing `round-N.json` is left in place until a new assessment succeeds. If sign-in is unavailable, Codex crashes, or both answers fail schema validation, the command reports that the round did not happen but the old accepted JSON remains at the canonical path, now potentially describing an earlier plan revision. Remove or quarantine the old output before beginning the forced attempt so a failed rerun cannot be mistaken for current evidence.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Stop treating planning workstreams as PR-backed**

Removing plan-review PRs leaves `/status-all` inconsistent: `core/.claude/skills/status-all/SKILL.md:212-218` still states that every workstream from `stage:planning` onward structurally has a PR and performs a targeted GitHub lookup before concluding it is unlinked. New in-session planning workstreams intentionally have no PR, so the status report will misclassify healthy planning work as missing/stalled unless that consumer is updated to use the issue labels/comments or local loop state.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Count PR-less plan loops in maintenance metrics**

The maintenance workflow still builds its rounds-per-loop inventory from merged implementation PR histories and closed `[PLAN REVIEW]` PRs (`core/.claude/skills/maintenance/SKILL.md:165-170`). Under this change, new plan rounds exist only in ignored local files and a mutable private Artifact page, while the implementation PR provenance records only the plan digest. Maintenance will therefore silently omit every new plan loop and understate review cost—the exact bias that the existing dual inventory was designed to prevent.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Pin the agreed oracle outside the mutable plan**

The normal round commands omit `--oracle`, so this fallback reads the oracle from the same plan file the builder rewrites after every review. Nothing compares its digest with round 0 or refuses an altered `plan-oracle` block; deleting a requirement from both the plan and that block therefore makes the next reviewer evaluate against the rewritten intent rather than David's agreement. Persist the round-zero oracle independently and require every later round to use or match that immutable value.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Exclude blocking review statuses from convergence**

This stop rule ignores `review_status`, so a schema-valid assessment with `review_status: "Repo context required"`, no required revisions, and reconciled priors satisfies the stated convergence condition even though the reviewer explicitly could not inspect enough of the repository to review responsibly. The same issue applies to a round requiring human clarification. Require an appropriate non-blocking status in addition to the two existing conditions, or route blocking statuses to their explicit escalation path rather than the approval close-out.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Remove live GitHub instructions from the retired surface**

This section declares the GitHub plan-review surface retired, but the same canonical contract still tells reviewers that Claude opens a draft PR (`lines 18-22`), describes re-reviews shown as GitHub diffs (`lines 43-44`), preserves GitHub-only status/output limitations (`lines 72-98`), and says never to implement on the plan-review PR (`lines 99-100`). `agents-core.md:131-150` likewise still routes plan reviews specifically from `[PLAN REVIEW]` PRs. Because `plan-review.mjs` injects this entire contract into every local round, the reviewer receives mutually inconsistent transport and output instructions; complete the migration instead of retiring only the final output subsection.

These documented commands run `plan-review.mjs` in the foreground, and the script uses `spawnSync` with a 45-minute timeout. The newly added `codex-cli-in-container.md:50-72` records that a measured Astra round took 522 seconds and that long runs need `setsid nohup` plus an exit file because the surrounding Bash tool call can end first. In that measured scenario the operational recipe can kill the reviewer and lose the round; provide a detached launcher/poller or make the script manage asynchronous execution itself.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Prevent private plan files from being staged**

The disclosure guarantee here depends on the plan never being committed, but only `.agents/reviews/` is ignored; `docs/plans/PLAN_<SLUG>.md` is not covered by any `.gitignore` or staging guard in this repository. A routine broad staging command such as `git add docs/` or `git add -A` during implementation will therefore include the supposedly private plan and publish any vulnerability, customer, or embargo details it contains. Add an enforceable ignore/guard or store the working plan under the already ignored review directory rather than relying solely on agent discipline.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restrict reviewer identity and sandbox overrides**

Although the constants describe Astra/xhigh/read-only as settled and overridable only for smoke tests, the production CLI accepts arbitrary `--model`, `--effort`, and even `--sandbox danger-full-access`, and the usage text advertises them. A normal loop invocation can therefore silently substitute a weaker reviewer or grant the reviewer write access to the live checkout, defeating both the independent-review identity and the read-only guarantee. Remove these public overrides or require an explicit test-only gate and scratch checkout before honoring them.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Represent safe-to-defer findings in the schema**

The canonical contract requires reviewers to separate `safe-to-defer` items from required revisions and recommended improvements (`plan-review-contract.md:402-409`), but this schema exposes only `recommended_improvements` and rejects additional top-level properties. On the new schema-constrained transport, a reviewer must therefore omit safe deferrals or misclassify them into another category, so the full assessment cannot satisfy its own contract. Add the missing section or explicitly fold and rename the contract category.

When an earlier `round-N.json` contains `scope_concerns` or `required_revisions`, passing `--no-prior` skips this refusal without inspecting that file, so the next reviewer can return `previous_findings: []` and satisfy `convergence()`. Fresh evidence after the prior reconciliation fix is that `reconciliationProblems()` compares only against the caller-supplied `priors`; this escape can therefore bypass both the input and output checks. Derive the expected IDs from the stored assessments and accept `--no-prior` only when they actually contain none.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Authenticate extension grants before increasing allowance**

Any loop driver can create `extensions.json` with `kind: "adjudicator"` or `kind: "david"`, and this validation accepts that claimed authority based only on shape and a nonempty reason; `allowanceFor()` then opens the requested rounds, including arbitrarily many for a claimed David grant. Fresh evidence after the budget fix is that the current skill still promises a `review-loop-record.mjs` record and committed `loop-extension-<pr>-<n>.json`, while `review-loop-adjudicator.md:114-115` accepts only that GitHub-derived record and the generator requires a PR, so no PR-less mechanism binds this file to either decision maker. Require a mechanically produced adjudication/David record rather than trusting a hand-written `kind`.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Pin the loop tier across rounds**

The allowance is recomputed from the caller's `--tier` on every invocation, with no comparison to the tier used by earlier rounds. An internal loop that reaches its round-3 cap can therefore invoke round 4 as `--tier product` and receive a five-round allowance without an extension adjudication, contradicting the scope gate's fixed ceremony tier and bypassing the internal budget. Persist the tier on the first budgeted round and refuse later changes unless they follow an explicit reclassification path.

In any consumer that already has `docs/plans/.gitignore`, this early return never verifies that it ignores `PLAN_*.md` (or anything at all), so a subsequent `git add -A` can still publish the private plan. Fresh evidence after the staging fix is that the enforcement applies only when no ignore file exists; append a managed pattern or verify the existing patterns instead of treating file existence as protection.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Record oracle changes only with a completed attempt**

`pinOracle()` rewrites `oracle.txt` before budget, prior, override, existing-round, dry-run, and sign-in checks run. Consequently an `--oracle-changed` invocation that is later refused—or exits 2 without sign-in—silently makes the new oracle authoritative, and the next successful invocation reports it as matching rather than stamping the reason promised by the skill. Fresh evidence after the oracle-pinning fix is this preflight mutation; stage the changed pin and commit it together with the round metadata instead.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Remove stale metadata during forced reruns**

A forced rerun deletes only `round-N.json`; if the subsequent sign-in check fails, execution returns before rewriting `round-N.meta.json`, leaving the previous accepted/converged metadata and old `planSha256` at their canonical paths even though the assessment was discarded. Fresh evidence after the prior forced-rerun fix is that the skill explicitly consumes metadata for convergence and provenance, so delete or quarantine the metadata and last-message artifacts alongside the JSON before starting the attempt.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Read the review contract from an immutable revision**

When the checkout contains an uncommitted edit to `plan-review-contract.md`, this function reads those mutable bytes and the prompt tells the reviewer to open that same working-tree path, while `contractDigest` merely records the result and validates nothing. A plan author—or a plan in this handbook that concerns the review machinery itself—can therefore weaken the review rules before launching a round, defeating the script's stated independence boundary. Read the contract from the committed revision or snapshot and pin its bytes for the loop.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep sensitive loop-close records off public issues**

This close-out step unconditionally puts the plan-loop trail in a workstream issue comment, but sensitive/disclosure-carve-out workstreams deliberately have no public issue—only a private draft Project item. In that context the instruction is either impossible, causing maintenance to lose the only durable rounds-run source, or encourages creating/posting to a public issue and disclosing the material the carve-out protects. Define a private durable destination for these loop-close records and teach maintenance to read it.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid re-asking after Codex execution failures**

When `codex exec` times out, crashes, or exits nonzero, this branch records the process error but leaves `assessment` null, so the loop immediately launches attempt 2 as though the first response merely failed schema validation. With the default timeout, one unreachable or hung reviewer can therefore consume another 45 minutes, and the generated re-ask falsely says there was a prior assessment to correct even though `text` is null. Restrict the re-ask to parse/schema/reconciliation failures and terminate the round after execution failures.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Do not mark rejected scope assessments as converged**

For round 0, a schema-valid assessment with `review_status: "Scope is wrong"`, `should_this_exist: "No"`, and an empty `scope_concerns` array produces `converged: true`, because only the two context/clarification statuses are treated as blocking. The command then prints `CONVERGED — the stop rule is met` for a reviewer explicitly recommending that the work not exist, which can send the scope gate down the approval path. Handle round-0 decision statuses separately or require a positive scope verdict before reporting convergence.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Enforce a fresh lens on every re-review**

The CLI accepts a missing `--lens` on every round and never compares a supplied lens with earlier rounds' metadata, so a re-review can be prompted with `No particular angle was requested` or repeat the same angle indefinitely. That makes the contract's required fresh attempt to invalidate the plan unenforceable precisely in the scenario it identifies—a reviewer repeatedly missing the same major issue—and such a round can still be declared converged. Require a nonempty lens on re-reviews and reject one already recorded for this loop.

In a consumer that already has `.agents/reviews/.gitignore` but does not ignore the whole directory, this existence check skips all enforcement, so `git add -A` can stage the prompt containing the full oracle, the assessment, and the metadata. Fresh evidence beyond the earlier `docs/plans/.gitignore` fix is that `ensureRoundDir()` still trusts its corresponding pre-existing ignore file; verify or append a managed `*` rule here as `ensurePlansIgnored()` now does.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Clear the completion sentinel before each detached round**

On every round after the first, `$S/run.exit` already exists from the previous invocation, but this command never removes it and the following instruction waits only for the file to appear. The waiter can therefore immediately read the old exit status while the new 9–10 minute review is still running, then proceed using stale output; remove the sentinel before launching or use a round-specific exit file.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Keep dry runs from changing the pinned oracle**

With `--oracle-changed ... --dry-run`, this call still replaces `oracle.txt` even though no assessment or metadata recording the reason is produced; the next real run then sees the changed oracle as an ordinary match. Fresh evidence after the earlier preflight-mutation fix is this explicit `pin.commit()` in the dry-run branch, contradicting the nearby invariant that the write occurs only when a round completes.

A schema-valid round-0 response with `should_this_exist: "Yes, but narrower"` and no `scope_concerns` passes this check and is reported as `CONVERGED`, even though the reviewer explicitly says the agreed boundary must be narrowed before planning. Include this enum value among the non-converged scope verdicts, just as `No` and `Not yet` are handled.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Invalidate later rounds when force-rerunning history**

When `--force` reruns an older round, this removes only that round's artifacts and leaves every later `round-N.json` and converged metadata in place, although those assessments were produced from the superseded plan and reconciliation chain. For example, replacing round 1 after round 3 converged leaves round 3 looking like valid current evidence; refuse non-latest forced reruns or discard all later rounds as well.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate nonempty evidence for required revisions**

When Astra returns a required revision with an empty `acceptance_check` or `evidence: []`, this schema and the local validator accept it because they enforce only field presence and types. Such an ungrounded, non-actionable finding can still hold the loop open and be carried into later rounds despite the prompt requiring inspected evidence and a pass/fail check; enforce nonempty strings and at least one nonempty evidence entry before accepting the assessment.
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Move converged workstreams to plan approval**

When the approval ask is posted, this recipe changes only `waiting:david` and never moves the issue to `stage:plan-approval`. The canonical ownership table in `core/docs/ai-context/workstream-tracking.md:344-348` explicitly assigns that convergence/close-out transition to `plan-review-loop`, so following the new skill leaves the Project reporting the workstream as still planning until it jumps directly to coding after approval.
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Honor zero-round grants as terminal stops**

When an adjudicator or David records a zero-round grant before the base cap—for example after the documented `escalate` dispatch at any round—this `Math.max` leaves the original tier allowance intact, so subsequent rounds remain permitted. That contradicts the skill's statement that `grant: 0` endorses stopping and the existing code-loop semantics in which a zero grant is terminal; represent the stop explicitly and refuse any later plan-review round.
